stories.headline: US AND IRAN TRADE FIRE IN HORMUZ AS MOU NEGOTIATIONS REACH CRITICAL JUNCTURE
stories.body: US and Iranian forces exchanged fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday — each side claiming the other shot first — even as envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner negotiate a 14-point MOU to end the conflict. The memo would declare a ceasefire, open a 30-day negotiation window, and begin sanctions relief discussions. The May 31 deadline holds Brent near $100 and keeps geopolitical risk premium embedded in every risk-asset price.

stories.headline: APRIL PAYROLLS CRUSH ESTIMATES: 115K JOBS ADDED VS. 62K FORECAST
stories.body: The U.S. economy added 115,000 jobs in April — nearly double the 62K consensus — while March was revised up to 185K. Wage growth softened to 3.6% YoY (vs. 3.8% expected), moderating the bond selloff. The data is Warsh's first major test as Fed Chair and drives CME hike odds to 38.5% for the next 12 months, cementing higher-for-longer through at least Q4 2027.

stories.headline: AMD +16% ON 57% DATA CENTER SURGE, LIFTING AI INFRASTRUCTURE TRADE TO ALL-TIME HIGHS
stories.body: AMD reported Q1 revenue of $10.25B (+38% YoY) with data center sales of $5.8B (+57%), driven by the Instinct MI400 AI GPU line. Shares surged 16-19% on the week to $415, lifting Nvidia (+2%) and SMCI (+13%) to fresh records. The S&P 500 hit 7,392 Friday — a sixth straight weekly gain — with AI infrastructure a primary driver of the 2026 equity rally. AMD guides Q2 revenue to $11.2B (+46% YoY).

stories.headline: WTI $95, BRENT $100 HOLD AS FRESH HORMUZ SKIRMISHES REINFORCE OIL RISK PREMIUM
stories.body: Oil prices held near multi-year highs on Saturday even as ceasefire negotiations progressed, with new Hormuz exchanges reinforcing market skepticism of a near-term resolution. WTI at $95.46 and Brent at $100.54 embed an estimated $10-15 geopolitical risk premium above supply/demand fundamentals — adding roughly 0.4-0.5 percentage points annually to headline CPI and compounding the Warsh Fed's inflation challenge heading into the June 17-18 FOMC.

stories.headline: NCAA VOTES UNANIMOUSLY TO EXPAND MARCH MADNESS TO 76 TEAMS STARTING 2027
stories.body: Both men's and women's tournament committees voted unanimously this week to expand the field from 68 to 76 teams beginning in 2026-27. The new Opening Round adds 12 games over two days before the traditional First Four, unlocking $131M in additional revenue distributions funded by new beer, wine, and spirits sponsorship deals — a first for the NCAA. Michigan won the 2026 men's title; the expanded 76-team bracket tips off March 2027.

stories.headline: KNICKS LEAD 3-0 AFTER 108-94 WIN; WEMBY DROPS 39 IN SPURS' 2-1 SERIES LEAD
stories.body: On Friday, Jalen Brunson (33 pts, 9 ast) led New York to a 108-94 road win at Philadelphia, putting the Knicks within one win of a Conference Finals berth. In the West, Victor Wembanyama posted 39 points, 15 rebounds, and 5 blocks to lift San Antonio over Minnesota 115-108 and take a 2-1 series lead. Saturday slate: Detroit-Cleveland Game 3 at Rocket Arena (DET leads 2-0) and OKC-Lakers Game 3 at Crypto.com (OKC leads 2-0).

stories.headline: SEAHAWKS HOST 2026 SEASON OPENER SEPT. 9 AS DEFENDING SUPER BOWL CHAMPIONS
stories.body: The NFL confirmed the full 2026 schedule releases Thursday, May 14 at 8 PM ET on NFL Network and ESPN2. The Seattle Seahawks — Super Bowl champions after their win over New England — host the league opener on Wednesday, Sept. 9 on NBC. Jaxon Smith-Njigba signed a 4-year, $168.8M extension this offseason; OTAs begin May 26. The 49ers and Rams play the league's first game in Australia (Melbourne Cricket Ground, Sept. 10).

stories.headline: TEXAS TECH QB BRENDAN SORSBY UNDER GAMBLING PROBE, DEPTH CHART IN FLUX
stories.body: Texas Tech's depth chart is unsettled after news of a gambling investigation involving starter Brendan Sorsby, adding uncertainty to the Red Raiders' pre-season preparations. Nationally, CBS Sports' updated CFP projections have Texas atop most polls with Arch Manning healthy, while Notre Dame and BYU stand out as the only two FBS programs returning at least 60% of their defensive snaps across all three position groups entering fall camp.

deepDive.title: The Hormuz Risk Premium — How Geopolitics Gets Priced Into a Barrel of Oil
content: US and Iranian forces exchanged fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, with each side claiming the other provoked first. WTI crude sits at $95.46 and Brent near $100 — levels that add an estimated 0.4-0.5 percentage points to annualized headline CPI and directly complicate the Warsh Fed's path at the June 17-18 FOMC. The paradox is that oil hasn't collapsed despite active ceasefire negotiations. Understanding why requires understanding how geopolitical risk premiums actually work: markets don't price the base case, they price the distribution of outcomes, and the right tail — a prolonged Hormuz closure — is catastrophic enough to sustain a persistent premium in the forward curve even while diplomats talk.

The Hormuz premium exists because of what the strait physically is: a 33-mile-wide chokepoint through which roughly 20% of globally traded oil transits daily, including 75-80% of Gulf crude exports destined for Asia. There is no short-run alternative route. Rerouting tankers around the Cape of Good Hope adds 15-20 days of transit per voyage — the equivalent of temporarily removing millions of barrels from the effective global supply, while permanently bidding up tanker day-rates. The IEA estimates a full closure would remove 15-17 million barrels per day from supply within weeks. IEA member Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases could cover 4-5 mb/d for roughly 90 days — meaningful, but not a replacement. The current $10-15 risk premium over fundamentals reflects this asymmetry precisely: a deal sends WTI to $75-80; a breakdown sends it to $115 or higher.

Historical analogues clarify the timing risk, not the magnitude. The September 2019 drone attacks on Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq and Khurais facilities knocked out 5.7 mb/d — roughly 5% of global supply — overnight, causing Brent to spike 15% at Monday's open. Prices fully retraced within two weeks because the disruption was geographically bounded and the production recovered. The Hormuz scenario is structurally different: it's a transit chokepoint, not a production site, so additional Saudi or Emirati pumping cannot solve the problem while the strait remains contested. The better analog is the 1973 Arab Oil Embargo — a transit and supply restriction that combined to quadruple oil prices over six months and drove US headline CPI above 12%, triggering a recession and forcing the Fed's hand in a way that haunted policy credibility for a decade.

The practical implication for the current setup: Warsh inherited a Fed caught between two bad outcomes. Cut rates to insure against a demand shock from protracted conflict, and you risk a 1970s-style policy error where oil-driven headline inflation embeds into wage expectations. Hold or hike to defend credibility, and you risk breaking something in credit markets while geopolitical uncertainty already suppresses capex. The May 31 MOU deadline is the most important macro binary of the next three weeks. A deal that credibly reopens the strait would likely send WTI back toward $78-82, remove a full percentage point from 12-month inflation expectations, and hand Warsh a disinflationary window to maintain policy optionality into Q3. A breakdown makes the June FOMC near-impossible to navigate cleanly — and raises the non-trivial probability of an unscheduled emergency meeting, something the Fed has done only six times since 2000.
